clue.text: Dark horse that may be last in Derby literally?

definitions.meaning: a dark horse is a person or thing whose abilities nobody knows in advance

definitions.text: that may be last in Derby literally?
definitions.meaning: the final letter of the word Derby is Y, which algebra uses for a value yet to be found

explanation.surface: A racing tipster wonders whether an outsider might finish at the back of the Derby, England's famous flat race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'literally' tells you to look at the letters of 'Derby' rather than the race: its last letter is Y, and x, y and z stand for unknowns in algebra.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark horse is a competitor nobody can size up, just as an algebraic variable has a value nobody yet knows.

clue.text: More than reasonable fare to Jupiter or Mars?

definitions.text: More than reasonable fare to Jupiter or Mars?

parts.words: More than reasonable fare to Jupiter or Mars?
parts.note: Jupiter and Mars are Roman gods rather than planets here, and their food is a divine, more-than-merely-acceptable dish

explanation.surface: It reads like a complaint about the price of a ticket for a space trip to the planets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fare' looks like a travel price but means food, and Jupiter and Mars are gods, not destinations. 'More than reasonable' hints that this food is better than decent: it is heavenly.
explanation.definitionFit: In classical myth the gods of Olympus ate this food, which gave them immortality.

clue.text: Bark perhaps coming about the Spanish hold at sea

indicators.note: coming about means going round something, so one piece wraps the other here

parts.note: to bay is to bark, as a hound does; 'perhaps' marks it as one kind of barking
el is the Spanish word for 'the'

explanation.surface: A sailing ship, a barque, turns about to hold its position at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bark' looks like a sailing ship, which suits 'coming about' and 'at sea', but it is the dog's noise, BAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors belay a rope by winding it around a cleat or pin to make it fast, so it holds.

clue.text: Delicacy is mixed with forage

indicators.note: mixed means stirred together, so the letters of the words named are reordered

explanation.surface: A fine dish turns out to be blended with animal feed.
explanation.definitionFit: Fattened goose or duck liver is a luxury food served as a treat in French cuisine.

clue.text: Entertainer stumped amid derisive hoot

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a jeer is a mocking shout
ST is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for stumped, a way a batter is out

explanation.surface: A performer is left lost for words as the audience jeers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stumped' reads as baffled, but on a cricket scorecard it is ST, a batter put out by the wicketkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: A court fool was employed to amuse a royal household, a kind of entertainer.

clue.text: Soldier dropped in wearing suitable American equipment

indicators.note: a soldier wearing something has it around him, so those letters go round the soldier

parts.note: apt means suitable
a para is a paratrooper, a soldier dropped from the air by parachute

explanation.surface: A paratrooper lands in the right American kit.
explanation.definitionFit: Apparatus is the gear or machinery needed for a job, so it means equipment.

clue.text: Brill for each coming aboard U-boat

indicators.note: coming aboard a vessel means getting inside it, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: a U-boat is a German submarine, a sub
per means for each, as in 'per head'

explanation.surface: A brill, a flatfish, is handed out to every sailor on a submarine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brill' looks like the fish, which suits the boat, but it is British slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Brill is British informal shorthand for brilliant, meaning excellent or first-rate.

clue.text: It prevents rocky ground becoming really stony

indicators.note: ground means crushed into pieces, so the letters are broken up and remade

explanation.surface: Something stops stony soil from being worn down any further.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocky' and 'stony' look like geology, but 'stony' is British slang, short for stony-broke: penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: Stony-broke means having no money at all, so really stony describes someone utterly destitute.

clue.text: Hit the XO?

definitions.meaning: a hit record that tops the charts
XO stands for executive officer, a ship's second-in-command, called by that nickname in the navy

explanation.surface: It looks like an order to strike someone, or to kiss and hug, since XO also means kiss and hug.
explanation.definitionFit: A chart-topping single is the top hit; and a naval first officer is addressed by that title.

clue.text: Left in place old Disney character

indicators.note: in puts the first piece inside the second

parts.note: to put is to place

explanation.surface: An old cartoon figure from Disney was left where it stood.
explanation.definitionFit: Mickey Mouse's dog first appeared in Disney cartoons in 1930, an old animated figure.

clue.text: Getting back to Coleridge, rating rushed over to tell story

indicators.note: getting ... over means turning round, so the whole string is read backwards
over joins 'Getting' to say the letters are turned the other way
the back of a word is its final letter, here the end of Coleridge

parts.note: a rating is a naval sailor of no rank, a tar
ran means rushed

explanation.surface: Getting back to Coleridge, a sailor dashes over to tell his tale, as in the Ancient Mariner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back to Coleridge' gives only the final E of that name; 'Getting ... over' then turns the whole string round. 'rating' is a naval sailor, echoing Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner, a seaman telling his story.
explanation.definitionFit: To narrate is to give an account of events, recounting a tale in order.

clue.text: On the gin, read out letters in swinging bar

indicators.note: in an across answer one piece on another comes after it

parts.note: a gin is a snare for animals, a trap

indicators.note: read out means spoken, so the word is written as it sounds

parts.note: letters are Es here: say the plural of the letter E

explanation.surface: A drunk on gin reads out letters while swinging on a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gin' looks like the drink but is a snare. 'read out' turns 'letters', the Es, into the sound EEZ, written EZE.
explanation.definitionFit: A circus trapeze is a horizontal bar hung from two ropes, swung on by acrobats.

clue.text: Launder western money initially neglected

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter, and neglected says it is dropped

parts.note: cash is money

explanation.surface: Money laundering in the West: the cash is ignored at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Launder' reads as money laundering, which suits the surface, but here it simply means clean clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To launder clothes is to clean them in water, a synonym for washing.

clue.text: British chatter about stray animal in stories

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: to rabbit, in British slang, is to talk on and on
to err is to stray from the right path

explanation.surface: British gossip about a lost creature from storybooks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rabbit' as chatter is British slang, from rhyming slang 'rabbit and pork' for talk.
explanation.definitionFit: The trickster hare-like hero of the Uncle Remus folk tales is a famous storybook creature.

clue.text: Mysterious clues about protagonist with roving eye

indicators.note: about means around, so the shuffled letters go round the next piece
mysterious means puzzling, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: a hero is the leading character of a story

explanation.surface: A mystery novel drops cryptic clues about its wandering-eyed main character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mysterious' jumbles the word clues, and 'about' then wraps the jumbled letters, split in two, round the protagonist.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with a roving eye keeps looking lustfully at others, so the phrase describes a lustful person.

clue.text: Ducks missing Chandler's debut in Friends?

indicators.note: missing says a letter is taken out

parts.note: quackers is a playful name for ducks

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so the first letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Ducks appear in the TV sitcom Friends, but without Chandler's first appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Friends' looks like the sitcom, where Chandler is a character, but the Religious Society of Friends is the formal name of the Quakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the Religious Society of Friends, a Christian movement, are known by this nickname.

clue.text: Old pupil a bright one nothing escapes

indicators.note: escapes means gets out of, so these letters are removed

parts.note: luminous means bright, giving off light
I is the Roman numeral for one
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A former student is described as so clever that nothing gets past them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nothing escapes' reads as a sharp mind, but 'one' and 'nothing', I and O, both escape LUMINOUS.
explanation.definitionFit: A former student of a school or college is called by this Latin word for a pupil.

clue.text: An atmosphere dismissing current style is rebellious

indicators.note: dismissing means sending away, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: air is atmosphere
I is the physics symbol for electric current
chic means style or elegance

explanation.surface: A mood that rejects current fashion is rebellious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'current style' looks like fashion, but 'current' is I, the symbol for current, taken out of AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawless and defiant of authority, as rebels against order are.

clue.text: Transport ship in drama crossing area by Channel island

indicators.note: crossing means lying across, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Noh is classical Japanese drama
Sark is one of the Channel Islands

explanation.surface: A troop ship in a play sails across near a Channel island.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis it was the boat that carried Noah's family and the animals through the Flood.

clue.text: Fool about to get at chap almost drunk

indicators.note: drunk means tipsy, so these letters stagger into a new order
almost means not quite all, so the last letter of chap is dropped

explanation.surface: A tipsy man goes after someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To play the fool or behave in a silly, clowning way is the idiom's meaning.

clue.text: Medic introduced to swimmer in wasteland

indicators.note: introduced to means put inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: a tuna is a fish, a swimmer
DR is short for doctor

explanation.surface: A doctor meets a fish in a barren place.
explanation.definitionFit: The treeless frozen plains of the Arctic are a bleak, barren wilderness.

clue.text: Brexiter insulted loads empty gun with bullets

indicators.note: loads means fills, so one piece goes inside the other
empty means with the middle taken out, leaving the first and last letters

parts.note: ammo is short for ammunition, bullets

explanation.surface: An angry Brexit voter loads an empty gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brexiter insulted' is a sound definition: 'gammon' is a British insult for an older, red-faced Brexit supporter.
explanation.definitionFit: In British political slang the name of a cured ham is used as a jibe at pink-faced Leave supporters.

clue.text: Put together power ballad?

parts.note: P is the symbol for power in physics
an air is a tune or song, such as a ballad

explanation.surface: A power ballad is put together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'power ballad' looks like one phrase, a rock song, but it splits into P and AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: To pair things is to match or join them in twos, combining them.

clue.text: Composer wasting time in tourism

indicators.note: wasting means losing, so the letter goes

parts.note: travel is tourism, going places for pleasure

explanation.surface: A composer is wasting his time on tourism.
explanation.definitionFit: Maurice Ravel was a French composer, known for Bolero.

clue.text: So much French spirit causes outburst

parts.note: tant is French for so much
rum is a spirit, a strong drink

explanation.surface: Drinking so much French liquor leads to a fit of rage.
explanation.definitionFit: A tantrum is a sudden childish fit of temper, a burst of anger.

clue.text: Quintessential Scots girl endlessly seen in cricket club

indicators.note: seen in means appearing inside, so one piece goes inside the other
endlessly means without its end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: lassie is Scots for a girl

explanation.surface: A typical Scottish girl is spotted at a cricket club.
explanation.definitionFit: Classic means a perfect or typical example, the essence of its kind.

clue.text: You French with craftsmanship entering Estonian city

indicators.note: entering means going into, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: tu is French for you
art is skill or craft

explanation.surface: French craftsmen come to a city in Estonia.
explanation.definitionFit: Tartu is the second city of Estonia, home to its oldest university.

clue.text: One bearing fruit to relieve poor

indicators.note: poor means badly made, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A charity bears fruit by helping the poor.
explanation.definitionFit: This Mediterranean tree bears fruit pressed for oil, so it is one bearing fruit.
